ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: The widely used chemical bisphenol A (BPA) has been associated with several health effects. In recent years, many derivatives were developed to replace BPA although without thorough toxicological evaluation. Here, we employed a human embryoid body (EB)-based in vitro global differentiation and hepatic specification models, followed by RNA-seq analyses, to comprehensively study the potential developmental toxicity of six BPA replacements (BPS, BPF, BPZ, BPB, BPE, and BPAF), as compared to BPA. We found that those bisphenols may disrupt lineage commitment and lipid metabolism during early embryonic development. These effects mostly manifested via the dysregulation of HOX and APO family genes. Moreover, among the seven bisphenols analyzed, BPE seemed to have the mildest effects.

ce:section.ce:para: Bisphenol A (BPA) is one of the most commonly used raw materials in consumer goods (Vandenberg et al., 2012). Nevertheless, many studies have reported BPA is harmful to humans in that it can affect the neural system, lungs, liver, adipose tissues, reproduction, and so on (Spanier et al., 2014; Braun, 2017; Meng et al., 2019; Ziv-Gal et al., 2015; Rochester, 2013). Some studies have reported BPA could even affect embryonic development in zebrafish and mice (Mao et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020). As a result, restrictions on the use of BPA have been recommended worldwide (Baluka and Rumbeiha, 2016). Thus, many other bisphenols, with similar structures and properties as BPA, have been gradually applied in several industrial applications (Liao and Kannan, 2014; Jurek and Leitner, 2017; Liao et al., 2012; Cacho et al., 2012), regardless of them being potential health hazards. Those alternatives include bisphenols S (BPS), F (BPF), Z (BPZ), B (BPB), E (BPE), and AF (BPAF), which have been already detected in the environment and human bodily fluid/tissue samples, at low nanomolar or picomolar levels (reviewed in (Caballero-Casero et al., 2016)). For example, the levels in the environment for BPA, BPS, BPF, BPZ, BPB, BPE, and BPAF could be as high as 292.3 μg/L (equivalent to 1280.33 nM), 318 ng/L (1.27 nM), 90.2 ng/L (0.45 nM), 151 ng/L (0.52 nM), 8.46 ng/L (0.035 nM), 84.4 ng/L (0.40 nM), and 74.9 ng/L (0.22 nM) (Wang et al., 2020). In human serum samples, BPA, B, S, and AF could reach as high as 7.12 ng/mL (31.2 nM), 0.62 ng/mL (2.48 nM), 0.78 ng/mL (2.32 nM) and 11.94 ng/mL (49.27 nM), respectively (Caballero-Casero et al., 2016; Cobellis et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2018).

Many different in vivo and in vitro models are generally employed for toxicity screening. In particular, stem cell toxicology models, such as the ones based on mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs), human embryonic stem cells (hESCs), human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs), human neural stem cells (hNSCs), and so on, have become more and more popular (Gu et al., 2019; Dong et al., 2018; Yin et al., 2019; Schwartz et al., 2015). By taking advantages of the self-renewal and differentiation of stem cells, it is possible to assess toxicity with multiple different endpoints (Liu et al., 2017). More interestingly, hESCs can differentiate in vitro via 3D aggregates called embryoid bodies (EBs), which mimic the early stages of human embryonic development as it occurs in vivo (Faiola et al., 2015).

In this study, we utilized a human EB-based global differentiation model to investigate the potential developmental toxicity of BPA and six of its replacements, BPS, BPF, BPZ, BPB, BPE, and BPAF. We found that those compounds altered differentiation, and mostly stimulated the expression of lipid metabolism-related genes. Moreover, when we employed a specific hepatic differentiation model, we indirectly demonstrated that the bisphenols’ effects on lipid metabolism originated at the time of cell fate decisions, prior to liver specification.

The seven bisphenols were purchased from different companies: BPA (B0494) from TGI, China; BPS (103039) from Sigma-Aldrich, USA; BPF (D135041), BPE (04487), BPB (B135300), BPZ (B136485), and BPAF (H106097) from Aladin, China. Their CAS number, chemical formula, and structure information is shown in Table S1. Bisphenols were dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, 0231–500 mL, Amresco, USA) to prepare 10,000 × stock solutions, and stored at −20 °C. Working solutions were prepared by diluting stock solutions in media; the final concentration of DMSO was 0.01% in all controls as well as treatment groups.

H1 hESCs (WA01, National Stem Cell Bank c/o the WiCell Research Institute) were cultured in mTeSR1 medium (85850, STEMCELL Technologies, Canada) supplemented with 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin (15140-122, Gibco, USA), on Vitronectin (A14700, Gibco, USA)-coated tissue culture dishes (150288, Thermo Fisher Scientific, China), at 37 °C in incubators with humidified air and 5% CO2 (FORMA 3111, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). Medium was replaced daily. When cells reached about 90% confluence, they were passaged with a 1:9 ratio by using Gentle Cell Dissociation Reagent (07174, STEMCELL Technologies, Canada).

Confluent hESCs were digested into single cells with TrypLE Select Enzyme (A1285901, Gibco, USA) and seeded in our patented homemade agarose EB mold (patent number: ZL201821538823.X)-containing 60-mm tissue culture dishes (150288, Thermo Fisher Scientific, China) as 3.6 × 106 cells/plate. The medium consisted in complete E8 medium (05990, STEMCELL Technologies, Canada) supplemented with 10 μM Y27632 dihydrochloride (HY-10583, MedChemExpress, USA) and 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin. Cells formed homogenous aggregates after overnight incubation. The next morning, aggregates were collected and transferred into ultralow 6-well (one 60-mm dish into all the wells) plates (3471, Corning, USA) containing homemade Essential 6 (E6) medium (DMEM-F-12 (C11330500BT, Gibco, China), 64 mg/L L-ascorbic acid 2-phosphate sesquimagnesium salt hydrate (A8960-50G, Sigma-Aldrich, USA), 14 μg/L sodium selenite (S9133-1MG, Sigma-Aldrich, USA), 10.7 mg/L human holo-transferrin (T0665-100MG, Sigma-Aldrich, USA), and 19.4 mg/L insulin (I8830-1G, Solarbio China)), plus 1 ng/mL DNase (DN25, Sigma-Aldrich, USA), and 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin. This day was designated as differentiation day 0. The differentiation lasted for 21 days with medium changed every other day. Cells were treated with 0.1, 1, 10, and 100 nM bisphenols (or 0.01% DMSO control) from days 0 to 21; chemicals were refreshed daily.

The hepatic differentiation was according to a previous report (Mathapati et al., 2016) with modifications. Briefly, hESCs were dissociated into single cells and seeded into Matrigel (356231, Corning, USA)-coated 24-well-plates (3524, Costar, China) in mTeSR1 medium, supplemented with 10 μM Y27632 dihydrochloride, at the cell density of 1.35 × 105 cells/mL, 1 mL/well. hESCs were cultured for another day in mTeSR1 medium without Y27632 dihydrochloride. To induce differentiation, cells were incubated with RPMI 1640 medium (61870010, Gibco, USA), plus 2% B27 supplement (A1895601, Gibco, USA), and 3 μM CHIR99021 (S2924, Selleck, USA) for one day, and subsequently RPMI 1640 medium plus B27 supplement for one additional day, to obtain definitive endoderm. Then, the medium was changed to KO DMEM medium (10829018, Gibco, USA) plus 20% KSR (10828028, Gibco, USA), 1% DMSO, 1% NEAA (11140050, Gibco, USA), 1% GlutaMax (35050061, Gibco, USA), and 100 nM 2-mercaptoethanol (M8210, Solarbio, China) for 5 days, to differentiate into hepatoblasts. From day 8, maturation medium, which contained Leibovitz 15 medium (11415064, Gibco, USA), 8.33% FBS (35–076-CV, Corning, USA), 8.33% Tryptose Phosphate Broth (T8159, Sigma-Aldrich, USA), 0.5% Insulin-Transferrin-Selenium (41400045, Gibco, USA), 1% GlutaMax, 0.05 mg/mL ascorbic acid (A7631, Sigma-Aldrich, USA), 10 μM Hydrocortisone-21-Hemisuccinate (H4881, Sigma-Aldrich, USA), 100 nM Dihexa (HY-16969, MedchemExpress, USA), and 100 nM Dexamethasone (D1756, Sigma-Aldrich, USA), was used to obtain hepatocyte-like cells. All media contained 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin and were refreshed daily. For toxicity evaluations, cells were exposed to different concentrations (0.1, 1, 10, and 100 nM) of bisphenols, or 0.01% DMSO (solvent control), all along the 18-day differentiation process.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Total RNA extraction and quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) analysis
ce:section.ce:para: Total RNA extraction was obtained with the RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (74136, QIAGEN, Germany) for the 100 nM bisphenol treated groups (and control), or TRNzol Reagent (DP405-02, TIANGEN, China) for 0.1, 1, and 10 nM bisphenol treated groups (and control). RNA was reverse transcribed with the FastKing RT Kit (KR116, TIANGEN, China). Then, qPCR assays were performed by using a SYBR green PCR master mix (RR420A, Takara, Japan) on a QuantStudio 6 Flex System (4484642, Life Technologies, USA), as previously described (Yin et al., 2018). Relative gene expression was calculated with the ΔΔCt method using GAPDH as a reference, and presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM) from nine repeats in three independent experiments. All experimental procedures were according to the manufacturers’ guidelines. PCR primers are listed in Table S2.

Total RNA from undifferentiated hESCs and day 21 EB differentiation samples treated with 100 nM of each bisphenol (or 0.01% DMSO control) was extracted with RNeasy Plus Mini Kit. The cDNA library construction and sequencing were performed at Beijing Genomics Institute, using the BGISEQ-500 platform. Reads were filtered with Trimmomatic (v0.360), summarized with SOAPnuke (v1.4.0), and aligned to the reference genome, GRCh3.p11(hg38), with Bowtie2 (v2.2.5). The quantification of gene expression was done by RSEM with FPKM as readout. Hierarchical clustering and heatmap drawing were done with Multiple Experiment Viewer (MeV 4.9.0).

For principle component analysis (PCA), PC1, 2, and 3 were calculated by using all the genes detected in the RNA-seq samples with IBM SPSS Statistics 23, then PCA data were visualized with OriginPro 2017. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified as fold changes ≥ 2 and Q value ≤ 0.001 by using the DESeq2 package (version 1.26.0) in R, and visualized as MA plots. Gene ontology (GO, http://geneontology.org/) and Kyoto encyclopedia of genes and genomes (KEGG, https://www.genome.jp/kegg/) enrichment analyses were performed by using Database for Annotation, Visualization and Integrated Discovery (DAVID 6.8), and Excel (Microsoft Office 2016). RNA-seq data are deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database under the accession number GSE149753.
Statistical analysis was performed using the two-tailed, unpaired Student's t-test. Statistical significance is indicated in the figure captions.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Bisphenols’ effects on gene expression during global differentiation
ce:section.ce:para: We differentiated hESCs via EB formation for 21 days; the pluripotency markers OCT4 and NANOG were significantly down-regulated, while markers for the three primary germ layers, endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm, were notably up-regulated, as expected (Fig. S1). To assess the potential developmental toxicity of bisphenols, we performed global differentiation in presence of 100 nM BPE, BPAF, BPF, BPS, BPA, BPZ, and BPB (or 0.01% DMSO solvent control), for 21 days ( Fig. 1A). Those concentrations were previously proven to be non-cytotoxic (Liang et al., 2020). Then, we analyzed the effects of the treatments on some marker genes of the three germ layers. As shown in Fig. 1B, overall, we did not observe any significant and consistent bisphenols’ effect on those genes, except for a marked down-regulation of KRT14 after treatments with all the bisphenols but BPB. In fact, for example, while BPA increased the expression of FOXQ1 (endoderm marker) and decreased TFAP2 and KRT14 (ectoderm markers), without affecting TBX5 (mesoderm marker), BPZ seemed to negatively affect some endoderm (CXCR4), mesoderm (PDGFRA, PDX5, and GSC), and ectoderm (NGN1, KRT14, TFAP2, and OTX2) markers (Fig. 1B).

To thoroughly compare BPA effects with the ones from its six alternatives, and conclude whether BPA replacements were safer than BPA, we performed global gene expression profiling, by RNA-seq. For simplicity, we only sequenced samples treated with one bisphenol concentration (100 nM) (Fig. S2). We identified differentially expressed genes (DEGs), with fold changes ≥ 2 and Q values ≤ 0.001, between treatment and control groups ( Fig. 2 and Table S3). For all the seven bisphenols, the number of up-regulated DEGs was higher than that of decreased DEGs. Moreover, as shown in Fig. 2, the number of total DEGs for each bisphenol was: BPE, 103; BPAF, 60; BPF, 57; BPS, 185; BPA, 135; BPZ, 103; and BPB, 131. Interesting, BPA affected more genes than all the other bisphenols except BPS. However, the PCA plot of Fig. S2A revealed that BPA treated samples were not the furthest away from control group. In addition, the seven bisphenols’ samples seemed to cluster in two groups: one including BPE, BPAF, BPF, and BPS, and the other containing BPA, BPZ, and BPB (Fig. S2B). To furtherly analyze bisphenol DEGs, we employed MA plots to search for genes that were both highly expressed and markedly affected by each bisphenol during global differentiation. As shown in Fig. 3, APO family genes and some liver-related genes, such as AFP, FGA, FGB, FGG, TF, and SERPINA1 stood out.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Bisphenol dysregulation of lipid metabolism during global differentiation
ce:section.ce:para: To obtain more information on how bisphenols may interfere with development, we investigated the functional annotation of the DEGs for each single bisphenol treatment. As depicted in Fig. 4 and Table S4, KEGG enrichment analyses (pathways with Q value lower than 0.05) revealed there were no significant terms in BPE treated samples, while the remaining six bisphenols partly shared enriched terms, although with different ranking. More specifically, except for BPE and BPAF, the most enriched pathways were “cholesterol metabolism”, “fat digestion and absorption”, “vitamin digestion and absorption” and “mineral absorption”. In addition, infection and immunity related pathways (“complement and coagulation cascades”, and “staphylococcus aureus infection”) were also significantly enriched (Fig. 4). Interestingly, two signaling pathways occurred in some treated samples. “PPAR signaling pathway”, one of the major pathways regulating lipid metabolism (Lodhi and Semenkovich, 2014; Dubois et al., 2017) was enriched in BPF, BPS, and BPZ groups, while “hedgehog signaling pathway” was just enriched in the BPS samples. BPE and BPAF altered less pathways (zero and one, respectively) compared to the other bisphenols (Fig. 4). Overall, representative genes in enriched KEGG pathways (Table S4) were consistent with the dramatically affected genes in MA plots (Fig. 3).

Subsequently, we analyzed bisphenol DEGs against the Gene Ontology (GO) dataset and filtered significantly enriched terms with Q values lower than 0.05 (Table S5). Our results showed that all the bisphenols influenced many aspects during global differentiation, such as “regulation of embryonic development”, “regulation of heterotypic cell-cell adhesion”, “regulation of cytokine secretion involved in immune response”, and “lipase inhibitor activity”. Since most enriched pathways in KEGG analyses were related to lipid metabolism, we selected lipid-related GO terms for further analyses. As shown in Table 1, while BPE and BPAF significantly altered only “lipase inhibitor activity”, BPA and the other four bisphenols affected almost all chosen pathways. Overall, BPE and BPAF disrupted a lower number of GO terms, compared to the other bisphenols, consistent with KEGG analyses.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Bisphenols’ effects during hepatocyte-like cell specific differentiation
ce:section.ce:para: On the account of KEGG and GO results showing bisphenols preferentially to disrupt pathways related to lipid metabolism, we considered lineage specific differentiations to further investigate this aspect. The adipose tissue and liver are the major places carrying on lipid metabolism (Desvergne et al., 2006; Samanez et al., 2012). Thus, we examined the expression levels of our lipid metabolism-related DEGs in human adipocytes, and fetal and adult liver tissues from the GeneAtlas U133A, gcrma datasets (Su et al., 2004). As depicted in Fig. S3, most of those genes expressed more highly in the liver than adipocytes. Moreover, we selected the hepatic markers HNF4A, AFP, ALB, FGA, FGB, FGG, PROX1, TBX3, TTR, SERPINA1, APOA2, ASGR1, CYP3A4, and DLX3 (Mathapati et al., 2016), and the adipocyte genes PPARG, PPARGC1A, ADIPOQ, CEBPA, ELOVL3, LPL, LIPE, CYC1, and UCP1 (Ahfeldt et al., 2012) to investigate their expression in our bisphenol transcriptomics data. We observed higher expression changes for hepatic marker genes, especially AFP, SERPINA1, and APOA2, than for those of adipocytes, ( Fig. 5A), in bisphenol treated groups. Therefore, we selected hepatic specification over adipogenesis for further investigations.

We applied a small molecule protocol to differentiate hESCs into hepatocyte-like cells (Mathapati et al., 2016), for 18 days and in the presence of bisphenols (Fig. S4A). The hepatic specification was successful since the pluripotent gene OCT4 was down-regulated, while the expression of hepatic marker genes (HNF4A, AFP, ALB, FGA, FGB, and FGG) increased (Fig. S4B). Then, we collected day-18 samples and performed RT-qPCR to measure the expression levels of the six hepatic markers mentioned above, and six lipid metabolism-related genes (APOA1, APOA2, APOA4, APOB, APOC2, and APOC3). Those 12 genes were upregulated after bisphenol treatments during global differentiation (Table S3, and Fig. 5A). To our surprise, only a few markers, such as HNF4A and AFP, were significantly affected, whereas the six genes related to lipid metabolism were not (Fig. 5B). Thus, we chose additional genes which were significantly affected by at least three bisphenols during global differentiation in our RNA-seq analyses (Table S3), and validated them by RT-qPCR. The expression of those genes changed by several folds, and sometimes even 100 folds, in 100 nM EB differentiation samples (Fig. S5A). Interestingly, we observed some changes in the expression of those genes even when we treated the differentiating EBs with 0.1, 1, and 10 nM bisphenols, as compared to control (Fig. S5B). However, the expression of those genes barely changed during the hepatic specific differentiation (Table S6). Additionally, HNF4α protein levels and lipid content in day 18 liver differentiation samples were not significantly affected by pollutant treatments (Figs. S6 and S7). Taken together, our findings suggest that more than liver differentiation per se, bisphenols could alter early cell fate determination occurring before hepatic commitment.

In order to verify this hypothesis, we reanalyzed the significantly enriched GO terms resulted from bisphenol treated EB global differentiation. We realized many of them were related to embryonic development, such as “cell fate commitment”, “cell fate specification”, “developmental process” and “embryo development”, and affected by all the bisphenols except BPZ (Table S7). When we went a step further to check the genes involved in these pathways, we recognized numerous HOX family genes, the core regulators of embryonic development (Mallo, 2018; Pearson et al., 2005). Indeed, HOX genes’ expression changed distinctively during global EB differentiation (Fig. 5C).

Taking everything into consideration, bisphenols might disrupt very early stages of embryonic development, rather than late lineage specifications. Moreover, BPE showed milder effects compared to the other BPA-like compounds.

There is still uncertainty regarding the safety of BPA replacements, as more and more studies have suggested their potential toxicity (Chen et al., 2016). Here, we employed global differentiation as well as hepatic specification hESC-based models, to compare the potential adverse effects of BPA with those of six of its substitutes, during development. The aim was also to shed light on which bisphenols may be safer. Bisphenols disrupted several biological processes with various degrees.

The use of in vitro models to mimic human embryonic development as alternatives to animal assays for chemicals safety screening aiming at developmental toxicity, has been long advocated (Krewski et al., 2010). The EB-based global differentiation of hESCs has been demonstrated to mimic embryonic developmental and thus valuable in developmental toxicology (Faiola et al., 2015; Itskovitz-Eldor et al., 2000). Nevertheless, only a few studies have used human EBs for chemical safety screening (Guo et al., 2019; Krtolica et al., 2009; Mehta et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2013).

In our RNA-seq analyses, we observed that bisphenols’ DEGs were mostly up-regulated. In addition, BPS affected the greatest number of genes among all seven bisphenols (Fig. 2), which was consistent with our previous study (Yin et al., 2019). The seven bisphenols also mainly affected early embryonic development- and lipid metabolism-related processes (Fig. 4, and Table 1, S3, and S4). More importantly, our KEGG and GO analyses imply that BPE may be relatively safer than the other six bisphenols. There is evidence that lipid metabolic pathways, as well as lipid molecules themselves, contribute to cell fate specification during early development (Russo et al., 2018). Moreover, lipid metabolism disorders can affect fetal growth and development (Bowman et al., 2019; Xue et al., 2019). As a result, if lipid metabolism is disrupted during embryonic development, developmental malformations (Herman, 2003; Kelley, 2000; Jira, 2013) and a class of lipodystrophy syndromes (Akinci et al., 2000) may occur. Thus, it is possible that several reported adverse health effects cause by bisphenols might have originated from effects on lipid-related genes during early development (Fig. S8).

The above-mentioned results confirmed our previous studies reporting bisphenols’ effects on early stages of embryonic development as well as adipogenesis. In fact, 100 nM BPA, BPF, and BPS very similarly disrupted early cardiovascular and nervous system development during mouse EB global and neural differentiation (Yin et al., 2019). Furthermore, nanomolar BPA levels stimulated adipogenesis, but also osteogenesis, in a human mesenchymal stem cell differentiation model (Dong et al., 2018), and it increased the expression of lipogenic genes to influence lipid synthesis in mouse liver (Marmugi et al., 2012). Interestingly, BPF reprogrammed lipid distribution in mouse liver and kidneys (Zhao et al., 2018). Overall, our data confirm the association between bisphenols and obesity (Liu et al., 2019).

We also employed hESC-based hepatic specification to further investigate the effects of bisphenols on lipid metabolism (Fig. S3). Unexpectedly, bisphenols did not produce strong effects (Fig. 5B S6, and S7; Table S5), suggesting their adverse effects on lipid metabolism occurred as a consequences of lineage fate decision more than during hepatic specification. However, liver- and lipid metabolism-related genes, such as HNF4A, AFP, ALB, APO family members, and metallothionein family genes, were sharply up-regulated during global differentiation. Consistently, several studies also showed effects on the liver after BPA treatment (reviewed in Porreca et al. (2017)).

Infection- and immunity-related pathways like “staphylococcus aureus infection”, “complement and coagulation cascades”, “drug metabolism-cytochrome P450”, and “drug metabolism-other enzymes” were also significantly enriched in bisphenol treatment groups during global EB differentiation (Fig. 5). These data imply that bisphenols, as exogenous compounds, can activate the immune system. This is in line with other studies revealing how BPA, BPS, and BPF could cause immune disturbance (Yin et al., 2019; Qiu et al., 2018, 2019; Xu et al., 2016).

Our results showed that PPAR signaling was affected by BPF, BPS, and BPZ, while hedgehog cascade only enriched in BPS treatment group (Fig. 4). This confirmed a previous report in that BPS was able to activate PPARγ and induce lipid accumulation in primary human preadipocytes (Boucher et al., 2016). However, to the best of our knowledge, the association between PPAR and BPF/BPS was not described before. Interestingly, BPA-PPAR signaling interaction was validated by several studies, including the recent one reporting that BPA altered the mRNA and protein levels of PPARα, β, γ in mouse testes and liver (Sharma et al., 2019). For hedgehog signaling, our data confirmed that BPA could manipulate Shh signaling pathway to stimulate adrenal cell proliferation (Medwid et al., 2018), as well as our results during mouse EB differentiation in that BPA, BPF, and BPS significantly disrupted hedgehog signaling at day 6, while BPS also at day 9 (Yin et al., 2019). Therefore, even though bisphenols may dysregulate PPAR and hedgehog signaling during development, their biological significance remains partially elusive.

Another family of genes highly disrupted by bisphenols was HOX family. Similarly to our findings, one study reported that BPA treatment increased Hoxa10 expression levels through epigenetic alterations in the developmental programming of uterine estrogen response (Bromer et al., 2010). Another study also suggested that interference with Hoxa10 and Hoxa11 expression could reprogram the normal responsiveness of uterine stromal cells during early postnatal life after BPA exposure (Varayoud et al., 2008).

As far as the comparison among bisphenols is concerned, Pelch and colleagues reviewed the human, animal, and mechanistic toxicity data for 24 BPA analogues, including the six we selected. They showed that many BPA analogues could cause effects at concentrations similar to or lower than those of BPA; more specifically, BPS, BPF, BPAF, BPB, and BPE were linked to metabolic problems (Pelch et al., 2019). Usman and Ahmad summarized four emerging bisphenols (BPAF, BPB, BPF, and BPS) together with BPA and showed that they could also cause toxic effects, including genotoxicity, like BPA (Usman and Ahmad, 2016). The two above reviews advocated for better ways to comprehensively evaluate whether BPA analogues are safe. One of these alternative systems could be hESC-based global differentiation, to systematical assess chemicals’ health risks.

In conclusion, our findings suggest that BPA and its six replacements (BPE, BPAF, BPF, BPS, BPZ, and BPB) may disrupt embryonic development and lipid metabolism. We demonstrated that bisphenols most likely affect early cell fate determination stages, and as a result of that, lipid metabolism. Among those bisphenols, BPE may be a relatively safer replacement for BPA. However, we still need to shed light on the complete molecular mechanisms behind those effects.
